Orbit integration study · 18 October 2026

Direct forces and
interpolated grids

A controlled comparison of force accuracy, retained orbit statistics and CPU runtime, using the same physical galaxy models and Dopri8 integration scheme.

Float64 · Gaussian order 800200 reference periods · 50,000 samplesTwo galaxy models · Four orbit launches

Keep the direct evaluator.

Trilinear grids make individual force requests cheaper. At the agreed state tolerance of 1e-9, the fine grid requires far more adaptive steps, produces larger physical-energy drift and takes longer to integrate the measured orbits. A smoother interpolation method is a candidate for a future experiment.

Experimental direct-versus-grid comparison

This work is isolated on codex/force-grid-benchmarks, based on orbit integration commit 69b4c2e. It does not select a production evaluator or change configuration defaults.

Findings and recommendation

Retain the direct static evaluator. The fine trilinear grid has sampled relative force differences around 2.6e-4 and maximum normalized physical energy drift 4.0e-5 to 2.7e-4, versus 1.7e-8 to 6.4e-8 for direct integration. At the agreed state tolerance 1e-9, it also requires many more adaptive steps. The fine-grid whole-solve medians are about 1.40-1.52 times slower than direct evaluation, using the protected timing control for the final case. Coarse-grid medians are about 1.7-3.1 times faster, with much larger physical-energy differences.

Coarse grids offer a runtime saving with substantially larger numerical differences. These results do not support enabling this prototype as a production default. If interpolation remains the next numerical priority, investigate a smoother method, preferably deriving forces from one interpolated scalar potential, then repeat the same controls. Retain explicit error targets and the direct evaluator as the reference. This experiment does not determine the best possible grid method or validate DYNAMITE's exact table implementation.

Task list

  • [x] Implement and validate a benchmark-only, reflection-symmetric force grid with explicit domain rejection.
  • [x] Compare off-grid forces and synchronized timings at three resolutions.
  • [x] Compare matched 200-period orbits, retained intrinsic statistics, direct energy diagnostics, setup costs and warm execution; record results and limits.
  • [x] Recheck the noisy final-case timing in rotated order and export summary figures without discarding the original observations.

Prototype scope

The first experiment follows DYNAMITE's coordinate and storage choice: uniform grids in log radius, polar angle and azimuth within the positive octant; trilinear interpolation of log(-a_i/x_i); reconstruction as a_i = -x_i * exp(interpolated coefficient). It assumes a static, coaxial, reflection-symmetric model. Its axes are the model's intrinsic Cartesian axes. It is not a literal DYNAMITE port or a DYNAMITE runtime benchmark.

The source inspected is DYNAMITE commit 0bd10a9586936bf6b9bcfdcd3679477d812a01d0, legacy_fortran/interpolpotent.f90. DYNAMITE uses 640 radial by 64 by 64 angular nodes, moves angular endpoint samples inward, and evaluates the direct force outside the grid. This experiment instead rejects out-of-domain queries. Endpoint coefficients are evaluated with each positive coordinate at least 1e-7 * radius, a declared approximation to the symmetry-plane limit that is checked against direct axis/plane probes. No automatic fallback is provided.

The tabulated force need not be the gradient of one scalar interpolated potential. Energy diagnostics therefore always use the unchanged direct physical potential; they capture force interpolation effects as well as integration error. Parameter gradients and production configuration/model wiring are outside this experiment.

A table belongs to one fixed physical model and must be rebuilt when that model changes. Saved tables do not preserve an automatic-differentiation graph linking their values to model parameters. Parameter-gradient accuracy, cache invalidation across models, GPU performance, rotated components, central/orbit-domain coverage and a production boundary policy need their own validation before runtime integration.

Force protocol and results

Run date: 2026-10-18. Both the oblate and strongly triaxial six-Gaussian galaxy models include their unchanged Plummer black hole and NFW halo. Float64 and Gaussian quadrature order 800 are retained. Each model uses 4,645 fixed probes: 4,096 draws uniform in log radius/polar angle/azimuth with random octant signs, plus 61 radii on nine axial/planar/diagonal/near-axis directions. Radius covers 1e-5 to 200 kpc; these probes are shared across all grids and are not a complete parameter-domain validation.

Resolution Radial / polar / azimuth nodes Table size Maximum relative force error, oblate / triaxial Warm construction, oblate / triaxial
Coarse 80 / 12 / 12 0.264 MiB 0.3958% / 0.3936% 0.269 / 0.486 s
Medium 160 / 24 / 24 2.109 MiB 0.1002% / 0.1031% 1.812 / 1.854 s
Fine 320 / 48 / 48 16.875 MiB 0.02465% / 0.02507% 14.969 / 15.464 s

Errors compare against the order-800 direct evaluator, not an exact solution. They use vector norms, avoiding division by zero components on symmetry planes. The fine grid's 99th percentile relative error is about 2.0e-4 in both models. Increasing resolution reduces sampled force error by about four times per level. This is much larger than the direct evaluator's measured quadrature error and the 1e-9 state tolerance; those are distinct error sources.

Each timing uses the same 2,048 off-node queries, one first call and three synchronized warm repeats. Sequential compiled scans cost about 90.7 ms for direct forces and 3.0-4.3 ms for grids: about 21-30 times faster for this request pattern. Batched timings are also retained. Neither ratio predicts a complete orbit or production-library speedup.

Grid lowering/compilation, first execution, one warm rebuild, and table I/O are separated. Compiled kernels can be reused between models with the same structure; the second model's compilation entries therefore include cache reuse. Setup measurements are individual observations, not confidence intervals. The process peak resident memory is 1.205 GiB in the existing 4 GB, two-CPU Linux VM; no memory setting was changed.

The direct scalar/batch discrepancy reaches 1.14e-11 relative near the centre, consistent with cancellation-sensitive NFW arithmetic. It is recorded separately and checked against an explicit 1e-9 protocol bound, not treated as interpolation error or a physical acceptance threshold.

Full probes, forces, errors, timings, physical models and source/input hashes are retained in grid_forces.json. Raw tables and individual records live in ignored benchmarks/work/ directories.

Reproduce

Mount an explicit read-only checkout of the established tnt-dynamite-comparison repository. Choose fresh work/output paths:

docker --context colima compose run --rm --volume /absolute/path/to/tnt-dynamite-comparison:/comparison:ro dev python -m benchmarks.grid_benchmark --comparison-checkout /comparison --work-dir /workspace/benchmarks/work/grid-forces-new --output /workspace/benchmarks/results/grid_forces-new.json

--case, --resolution, --warm-repeats, --r-min, and --r-max select explicit variants; no automatic tuning, fallback, or output overwriting is performed. The model builder, exported launches, and provenance machinery are shared with benchmarks/orbit_checks.py; force timing functions are shared with benchmarks/gaussian_forces.py. Run scientific processes sequentially.

The orbit phase consumes those exact table files and verifies their hashes, specifications, physical model, numerical source files, library versions and comparison inputs. Use the same case selection as the force phase:

docker --context colima compose run --rm --volume /absolute/path/to/tnt-dynamite-comparison:/comparison:ro dev python -m benchmarks.grid_orbits --comparison-checkout /comparison --force-result /workspace/benchmarks/results/grid_forces-new.json --force-work-dir /workspace/benchmarks/work/grid-forces-new --work-dir /workspace/benchmarks/work/grid-orbits-new --output /workspace/benchmarks/results/grid_orbits-new.json

Orbit protocol

The four launches are the oblate outer box E5, strongly triaxial tube E3, strongly triaxial box E3, and strongly triaxial outer box E5. Every direct and grid solve uses the identical exported launch, DYNAMITE shell clock, random key, 200-period duration, 50,000 output times, float64, Dopri8, normalized tolerance 1e-9, and maximum one million adaptive steps. Each variant has one first compiled execution and three warm repeats. Compilation is measured separately and can reuse kernels between launches. The unchanged production solver is shared through a benchmark-only adapter; the public runtime API still rejects that adapter.

Whole-solve timings include uniform output samples and energy diagnostics at every sample plus the exact endpoint. Model creation, table loading, compilation, statistics and artifact I/O are recorded separately or excluded. The scalar direct potential is retained for all energy diagnostics: abs(E-E_launch)/V**2, where V is the existing launch/reference-clock normalization. These are not energy errors divided by initial energy and are not the solver's local state tolerance.

Retained statistics use the same intrinsic radial, Cartesian and velocity bins and moments as the direct-orbit benchmark. Histogram total variation is half the sum of absolute probability differences. These precede spatial symmetry operations, counter-rotation and observational projection. Split-half variation provides finite-window context rather than formal error bars. First-period position/velocity differences are normalized root mean square component differences; long-window pointwise agreement is not required for sensitive orbits. A further 2,000 uniformly indexed samples per direct orbit probe the grid forces along exactly matched physical paths.

Raw trajectories remain in ignored work directories. The portable orbit artifact retains full histograms/moments, diagnostics, repeated timings, force probes, artifact/source hashes and control differences. Timings and statistics do not assume a production library or an accepted interpolation error target.

The fine-grid solves require 15.5-16.8 times as many total adaptive steps as direct integration. About 51-70% of grid step attempts are rejected. The force is continuous but its derivatives change at interpolation-cell boundaries. Increased adaptive stepping erodes the cheap-force advantage; we have not profiled the individual sources of per-step overhead.

Fine-grid first-period position and velocity RMS differences remain below 1.5e-4 in launch-normalized units. Along the 8,000 uniformly indexed direct-trajectory points, the fine grid reaches maximum relative force difference 2.59e-4; the three resolutions produce another 24,000 matched force comparisons.

The outer-box spatial histogram differences are 14.01% (oblate) and 11.34% (triaxial) even at the fine resolution. Their direct split-half distances are 33.14% and 37.18%, respectively. The earlier order-1600 / accuracy-1e-11 controls gave 0% / 0.004% for the oblate box and 2.872% / 5.988% for the triaxial box. Split-half variation is not an acceptance threshold: it does not make a numerical difference acceptable. Time/sampling convergence and projected-observable error targets remain separate work.

Increased resolution improves force and energy diagnostics systematically; some long-window histogram distances are not monotonic. These observations do not formally classify any orbit as chaotic.

Setup and resource observations

Table loading and device transfer cost 0.006-0.149 s here, excluding the separately recorded hash verification. This cannot replace per-model table construction when physical parameters change. All setup and compilation observations remain in the portable artifacts; compilation can be reused between matching model structures. The full orbit matrix has process peak resident memory 1.100 GiB in the unchanged 4 GB, two-CPU VM.

The final direct outer-box timing series spans 14.89-93.17 s. Native host power logs show sleep overlapping late measurements; the first rotated-order control also contains a 63.03 s fine-grid observation. We cannot assign each outlier exclusively to sleep. Both original series are retained, and neither is treated as an isolated CPU performance measurement.

Build-only break-even estimates in the JSON divide warm grid-construction time by warm time saved per identical repeated launch. A null result means no warm solve saving was observed. They exclude compiler cost and accuracy acceptance and do not estimate production-library throughput.

Protected timing control

A second control repeats the final triaxial box E5 under a temporary native caffeinate -i -t 900 assertion, verified before and after the run. The host power log shows no new sleep event during that protected interval. No permanent power or VM setting was changed. The host-side verification and artifact hashes are retained in grid_timing_host_context.json.

Each control uses one compiled warmup per method, then three cycles with rotated evaluator order. All 16 solves per control reproduce the parent trajectory, times and diagnostics exactly. Across the main matrix and both timing controls, all 96 solves succeeded.

Evaluator Original matrix median [range] (s) First control median [range] (s) Keep-awake control median [range] (s)
direct 18.11 [14.89-93.17] 14.49 [13.70-20.63] 15.12 [14.66-18.74]
coarse 5.89 [5.64-7.08] 6.69 [4.84-7.37] 4.81 [4.75-5.05]
medium 25.90 [24.47-26.90] 20.79 [19.18-20.81] 17.38 [17.27-21.38]
fine 28.50 [26.16-30.09] 25.70 [23.09-63.03] 21.14 [19.62-21.79]

The protected medians are 15.12 s direct, 4.81 s coarse, 17.38 s medium and 21.14 s fine. Fine interpolation is about 1.40 times slower than direct evaluation in this control. Timings still vary with machine state; three repeats do not establish confidence intervals or universal performance ratios. Accuracy conclusions are independent of those wall-clock variations.

Both grid_timing.json and grid_timing_awake.json preserve all observations, compilation timings and source/parent hashes. Repeat the control with this macOS host command; on Linux, omit the native caffeinate -i prefix:

caffeinate -i docker --context colima compose run --rm --volume /absolute/path/to/tnt-dynamite-comparison:/comparison:ro dev python -m benchmarks.grid_timing --comparison-checkout /comparison --force-result /workspace/benchmarks/results/grid_forces-new.json --force-work-dir /workspace/benchmarks/work/grid-forces-new --orbit-result /workspace/benchmarks/results/grid_orbits-new.json --orbit-work-dir /workspace/benchmarks/work/grid-orbits-new --output /workspace/benchmarks/results/grid_timing-new.json

For future macOS measurements, use the same temporary host keep-awake wrapper around each long Docker benchmark command. The assertion ends with the command. A Linux guest cannot prevent its macOS host from idling by itself.

docker --context colima compose run --rm dev python -m benchmarks.plot_grid_results --forces benchmarks/results/grid_forces-new.json --orbits benchmarks/results/grid_orbits-new.json --timing-control benchmarks/results/grid_timing-new.json --output-dir benchmarks/figures/grid-new

Interactive HTML report

FORCE_GRID.html is the self-contained sharing version. It includes the complete written report, original PNG/PDF figures, interactive force/orbit/timing comparisons, and exact compressed copies of all five portable JSON artifacts. CSS, JavaScript and assets are embedded; no server or network request is needed. The orbit runtime view explicitly distinguishes original matrix observations from the protected final-case control. Large raw trajectory and grid-table files remain outside the portable report.

Rebuild into a fresh filename using the existing documentation environment:

docker --context colima compose run --rm dev python -m benchmarks.export_grid_report --output benchmarks/FORCE_GRID-new.html

The exporter uses markdown-it-py, already provided by the MyST documentation dependencies, and refuses to overwrite an existing file. Its editable layout is benchmarks/force_grid_report.html.in. Uncompressed JSON downloads use the browser's native gzip decompression; labelled .gz copies are also available. The report and interactive summaries do not depend on decompression support.

Validation

pytest -q tests/unit_tests/test_force_grid.py: eight tests passed in the Linux development container. They check analytic Plummer convergence and radial endpoints, Gaussian nodes/axes/planes and reflection symmetry, units, JIT domain rejection, unsupported models, and a circular-orbit comparison using the production solver with direct physical-energy evaluation. ruff check . and the Sphinx HTML build with warnings treated as errors passed. The full repository test suite was not run. An artifact audit verified all source/table/probe hashes, dtypes/shapes, timing medians, convergence and recorded errors. Independent SciPy linear interpolation agrees with the JAX grid on all 27,870 force comparisons to better than 1e-12 relative. These checks validate the implementation and retained artifacts, not final observable accuracy.

The orbit artifact audit verified all 16 variant hashes, source/input fingerprints, finite float64 output shapes, matched uniform clocks, physical parameters, repeated diagnostics, step counts, all-sample histograms/moments, control distances and first-period errors. All four new direct trajectories and their saved times are bitwise identical to the previous direct benchmark. The supplemental timing audit verified both controls' source/parent hashes, rotated orders, positive timings, retained observations/medians and host-context links. The exported scientific figure was visually inspected.
